Harcèlement de rue : les jeunes filles s: Street harassment: young girls just want people to “leave them alone”
Le court métrage est une initiative pour: The short film is an initiative to raise awareness about street harassment, a problem that disproportionately affects young women.
De gauche à droite: Sareena Kumari et Sa: From left to right: Sareena Kumari and Sanah Chourouhou. Photo credit: Vanroy
Pierre Gaillard, chargé de projet à la M: Pierre Gaillard, project manager at the Maison des jeunes de Bordeaux-Cartierville, invited La Converse to the screening of the short film Fiche-moi la paix !!! I find out about the invitation a few hours before the event is due to take place.
À la lecture de l’affiche annonçant la p: Reading the poster announcing the screening, I immediately thought it would be important for La Converse to report on this initiative, especially since <l1>projects documenting street harassment are rare in Quebec</l1>. It mattered to me to go meet the young girls and understand how they experience this reality in their own neighbourhood.
Ayant moi-même été victime de harcèlemen: Having been a victim of street harassment several times in my own life, and not knowing a single woman around me who has never experienced it, I felt it was worthwhile to shine a light once again on this persistent social issue.
Je tiens à préciser que nous étions le s: I should point out that we were the only media outlet present at the screening.
<strong>Vendredi 5 septembre. Au parc Mé: Friday, September 5. At Mésy Park, voices ring out over a game of basketball. Behind the court, smoke from a barbecue rises into the air. That evening, young people and staff from the Maison des jeunes de Bordeaux-Cartierville (MDJBC) are gathering to watch Fiche-moi la paix !!!, a short film by Sanah Chourouhou about street harassment. Bordeaux-Cartierville, far from being an exception on the island of Montréal, is grappling with this persistent phenomenon. A report on an initiative that seeks to raise public awareness of a reality that, sadly, is still treated as ordinary in 2025.
Alors que Sareena Kumari avait 15 ans, u: When Sareena Kumari was 15, a man stopped in front of the stop where she was waiting for the bus and asked her to get into his car. In another incident, while she was walking down the street, a man suddenly appeared on a bicycle, slid his hand under her skirt and then sped off. Now a coordinator at the MDJBC, she listens to the many young people who come to the centre and who, in turn, are experiencing this violence.
La Maison des jeunes a effectué un sonda: The Maison des jeunes conducted a survey of people living nearby, and the verdict was unequivocal: every single person surveyed said they had faced a situation of street harassment <l1>at least once</l1>. The alarm bell had rung, and the 26-year-old refused to remain a bystander.
C’est dans ce contexte qu’est né, il y a: It was in this context that the project sharing the short film’s name was born three years ago. As part of it, the MDJBC went into the neighbourhood’s high schools to highlight the consequences of street harassment.
Lancé en 2022 par Sareena Kumari, en col: Launched in 2022 by Sareena Kumari, in collaboration with Émile Ndikumagenge, director of youth services at the MDJBC, Fiche-moi la paix !!! is an initiative run with Prévention Montréal that aims to fight street harassment. The project focuses on raising awareness, providing resources and creating a safe space for young people. It involves offering workshops in high schools in the Bordeaux-Cartierville neighbourhood and, more recently, making a short film of the same name.
Jour de projection. Des chaises sont ali: Screening day. Chairs are lined up facing a podium where a microphone has been set down.
Les spectateurs se rassemblent dans le q: Spectators gather in the Bordeaux-Cartierville neighbourhood. Photo credit: Florence Aquilina
La mairesse de l’arrondissement Émilie T: Borough mayor Émilie Thuillier takes the floor and explains that many people see street harassment as an “unchangeable” reality. She stresses the importance of an initiative like Fiche-moi la paix !!! which, in her view, is proof that “no, it’s not normal; yes, things can change; and yes, it is possible to walk around in complete safety.”
Et puis, tout le monde se lève, traverse: And then everyone gets up, crosses the street and heads to the Centre culturel et communautaire de Cartierville, where the film is to be screened. Bags of popcorn in hand, the young spectators keep their eyes glued to the screen. One after another come the testimonies of young girls who have experienced various forms of harassment in the neighbourhood. From persistent, unsolicited catcalling to situations of real danger – a young girl followed by a drunk man – the stories pile up, both disturbing and revealing.
Nous demandons à Laurène, spectatrice de: We ask Laurène, a 16-year-old spectator who is also one of the people featured in the short film, for her reaction after the screening. “It really shows that street harassment isn’t something to brush off… I told myself I did the right thing by talking about it.”
Dans le documentaire, la jeune fille rac: In the documentary, the young girl says she has been a victim of street harassment several times, right in the Bordeaux-Cartierville neighbourhood itself.
« En tant qu’adolescente, tu te développ: “As a teenager, you’re developing, and that alone is a big change for you as a person. At the same time, the way other people look at us changes.”
Nous l’invitons alors à préciser sa pens: We ask her to explain what she means.
« Ça veut dire qu’en sixième année, ou m: “It means that in Grade 6, or even in high school, you’d wear leggings and nobody was looking at you in a sexualized way […] Now there are guys at school, and even teachers, who look at you like that. We just want to learn and get on with our lives, but it’s a pretty oppressive climate for young girls,” she laments.
<strong>Le risque est 22 % plus élevé po: The risk is 22% higher for racialized women
Apparaît alors à l’écran la sociologue I: Sociologist Isabelle Courcy then appears on screen. In 2022, she led and published <l1>a quantitative survey</l1> on street harassment in Montréal. In front of the camera, she discusses one of the study’s conclusions: visible minorities are at greater risk of experiencing street harassment. As the statistical portrait drawn up by the Université de Montréal professor reveals, 84.4% of racialized or Indigenous cisgender women have experienced harassment, compared with 62% of white people. That percentage climbs to 95% among racialized or Indigenous people who are part of the LGBTQ+ community.
Au-delà de l’ethnicité et de l’identité: Beyond ethnicity and gender identity, another risk factor is age. On this point, the study’s findings are clear: “The younger you are, the more you experience it.” The numbers speak for themselves, with as many as 91.4% of cisgender women aged 18 to 24 having experienced street harassment. And nearly half of those surveyed experienced it for the first time while they were still minors.
Nous demandons à Sanah Chourouhou – qui: We ask Sanah Chourouhou – who, in addition to being a documentary filmmaker, is a youth worker at the MDJBC and has been involved in the Fiche-moi la paix !!! project for two years now – why she thinks visible minorities are more at risk.
Elle répond : « Les minorités visibles s: She replies: “Visible minorities are the victims of our society. There are norms and codes, and when you step outside those norms, some people see you as more vulnerable and easier to criticize, like women, gender and sexually diverse people, and people with disabilities.”
Le documentaire se termine, l’écran devi: The documentary ends and the screen goes black. The question period begins; Sanah and Sareena field the questions. Several young people from the neighbourhood ask theirs. One last hand goes up: a young girl speaks up and asks with conviction, “What’s the solution to ending street harassment?”
Toujours selon l’étude de la professeure: Again according to Professor Courcy’s study, men are “the main perpetrators” of street harassment, although they can also be victims of it. For her part, while leading the awareness workshops, Sanah says she was struck by the misogyny of some of the boys. She explains that many of them attended voluntarily, but with values that were already deeply ingrained. She particularly remembers one group of young people in which some boys frequently made comments like: “It’s women’s fault and the way they dress!”
Certains repartent toutefois transformés: Some, however, leave transformed, she concludes.
Sareena, quant à elle, propose une solut: Sareena, for her part, proposes a legislative solution. “That would really be a big dream,” she says with a smile. “I’d like it to be dealt with at the level of the law. In France, they brought in a law in 2018. I think there should be penalties here too for people who harass.”
Sareena fait ici référence à la <l1>Loi: Sareena is referring here to the <l1>Loi Schiappa</l1>. Adopted in France seven years ago now under politician Marlène Schiappa, it aims to combat sexual and gender-based violence. Among other things, the law introduces the offence of “outrage sexiste” (sexist insult) so that street harassment can be penalized, punishable by a fine ranging from <l2>90 to 1,500 euros</l2> depending on the offence committed.
Il n’existe pas de mesure comparable au: There is no comparable measure in Quebec.
La soirée est terminée. Dehors souffle u: The evening is over. Outside, a light late-summer breeze is blowing. Everyone heads home. In front of the centre, the park and the streets are dimly lit. And we are reminded why this project exists: so that everyone can make their way home in peace, without having to quicken their pace, without having to look over their shoulder.
